name: searchsploit
plain: `searchsploit` searches a local copy of Exploit-DB, the public archive of exploit code and security papers. You give it a product and version you found with nmap, and it lists exploits that match.
It works offline, which is why it is handy in labs and on exam machines. It also copies an exploit file next to you so you can read and edit it before using it.
when: You found a service version with nmap -sV and want known exploits.
Look for a vulnerability by CVE or title.
Copy an exploit script to your working folder.
Read what an exploit does before running it.

examples.title: Search by product and version
examples.explain: Lists matching exploits with their title and path. Several words are ANDed together.

examples.title: Search a service from nmap
examples.explain: A well-known backdoor in one particular version. Compare the exact version number your scan showed.

examples.title: Exact phrase search
examples.explain: -e requires the exact phrase instead of any word order.

examples.title: Look at the code without copying
examples.explain: -x opens (examines) the exploit with its EDB-ID so you can read what it does.

examples.title: Copy an exploit to the current folder
examples.explain: -m mirrors (copies) the exploit file. Edit your copy, never the database.

examples.title: Search by CVE
examples.explain: Finds exploits that reference the given CVE.

examples.title: Take nmap's XML output
examples.explain: Reads an nmap -oX file and searches every detected service.

examples.title: Update the database
examples.explain: Pulls the newest exploit entries (needs internet).

options.plain: One or more search words; all must match.
Remove results matching these terms (separate with |).
options.use: Cutting noise like dos or Metasploit.

options.plain: Show the Exploit-DB web URL instead of the local path.
Show an exploit in the pager.
Copy an exploit into the current folder.
Show the full path and copy it to the clipboard.
Search from an nmap XML file.
Allow long titles to overflow the column.

mistakes: Searching with a long full banner: use the product and the first two version numbers.
Running an exploit without reading it: it may need editing or may do harm.
Editing the original file in the database: copy it with -m first.
Assuming a match means the target is vulnerable: check the exact version and conditions.
Using exploits on systems you do not have permission to test.
try: Search for vsftpd 2.3.4 and read the exploit with -x.
Copy it with -m and note what ports it uses.
Run searchsploit --nmap on one of your own scans.
see_also: nmap(1), msfconsole(1), curl(1), and exploit-db.com for the web view.
captured_with: Examples are written to explain a technique; they are not captured output.
